channel.title: Sustainability on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Sustainability on Best of AI

item.title: BeeHero
item.description:
In-hive sensors track temperature, humidity, vibration, and sound. In-field sensors count bee activity in crops. Data flows through a gateway to an analytics platform that flags weak colonies and helps schedule pollination.

BeeHero works with commercial beekeepers and growers, mainly in crops like almonds and blueberries. Reports of results come from the company, so growers should ask for trial data.

Hobbyists will find it too large in scale. BeeHero suits commercial beekeepers and pollination managers.

item.title: Global Fishing Watch
item.description:
Users see vessel tracks, fishing effort, and protected areas. Fishery managers and enforcement agencies use it to check activity near marine reserves and to spot suspicious behavior. Data downloads and an API support research.

Coverage depends on vessels broadcasting their position, so some boats are invisible.

Windward and Spire provide commercial maritime data. Global Fishing Watch suits fishery managers and conservation scientists.

item.title: HiveTracks
item.description:
Users keep a history for each hive, with guided inspection forms matched to their experience level. The app suggests when to inspect next and offers a bee weather forecast for choosing inspection days. It works on phones with offline use and syncs later.

The core app is free with paid upgrades. Reviews note that mite counts and reports are basic, so serious operations may want extra tools.

Spreadsheets and BeeKeeper-style apps are alternatives. HiveTracks suits hobby and sideline beekeepers.

item.title: Movebank
item.description:
Researchers upload tracks, annotate them with environmental data, and analyze or share them. A public map displays selected studies. It is run by the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior with partners.

Data access depends on each study’s sharing settings.

Wildlife Insights covers camera traps. Movebank suits wildlife biologists and zoologists who track animals.

item.title: Taranis
item.description:
Images from planes or drones are analyzed to find issues at the leaf level. Reports guide agronomists to problem areas. Insights integrate with farm management tools.

It is a commercial service with custom pricing.

DroneDeploy and Climate FieldView offer related imagery. Taranis suits crop consultants and agronomists.

item.title: Vintrace
item.description:
Winemakers log additions, analyses, and transfers, and see lot histories. Work orders guide cellar staff. Reports support tax and compliance filing.

It is a subscription product for commercial wineries.

Ekos and InnoVint are alternatives. Vintrace suits winemakers who run production at scale.

item.title: Persefoni
item.description:
Persefoni helps companies calculate and report their greenhouse gas emissions. It collects data from energy bills, travel, procurement, and suppliers, applies emission factors, and calculates totals for direct emissions, purchased energy, and value chain emissions. The system keeps an audit trail so figures can be verified.

Reporting is a main use. The platform produces disclosures aligned with frameworks such as the GHG Protocol, CDP, and regional regulations, and helps set and track reduction targets. An AI assistant answers questions about methodology and data, and supports tasks like mapping spend data to emission categories.

item.title: Pachama
item.description:
Pachama works on the trust problem in carbon markets. Credits from forest projects are only valuable if the forest is actually protected or restored, and checking this is hard. Pachama’s models analyze satellite and lidar data to estimate carbon stored in forests and to detect deforestation or degradation over time.

Buyers use its ratings and monitoring to choose credits and track them after purchase, and project developers use the data to support their claims. The company has also worked on tools for measuring forest carbon more cheaply than field surveys alone.

item.title: Patch
item.description:
Patch simplifies buying carbon removal. Companies browse projects, compare prices and methods, and purchase credits through a platform or API instead of negotiating deals one by one. Developers can embed purchases into other software, such as financial or e-commerce products.

The company has shifted toward helping enterprises plan and procure carbon removal at scale, with tools for sourcing, due diligence, and reporting. AI supports tasks like drafting requests for proposals and evaluating projects.

item.title: Sylvera
item.description:
Sylvera brings independent analysis to the carbon market. Analysts and models assess projects, such as forest protection or renewable energy, against criteria like additionality and permanence, and issue ratings. Satellite data and machine learning help measure forest carbon and detect deforestation.

Buyers use the ratings to choose credits, and sellers use them to demonstrate quality. The platform tracks market prices and supply, and supports due diligence.

Sylvera is sold on subscription to enterprises and financial institutions. Carbon markets remain contested, and ratings reflect methodology choices. Alternatives include BeZero Carbon, Pachama, MSCI Carbon Markets, Calyx Global, and Renoster. Sylvera suits buyers evaluating carbon credits.

item.title: Carbon Trust
item.description:
The Carbon Trust began as a UK organization set up to help businesses and the public sector cut emissions, and it now works internationally. It advises companies on how to measure their greenhouse gas emissions across operations and supply chains, set reduction targets, and plan the changes needed to meet them. Its work spans corporate carbon footprinting, product footprints, net zero strategy, and support with climate disclosure requirements.

A well-known part of its business is certification and standards. The Carbon Trust Standard recognizes organizations that measure and reduce their footprint, and other programs verify claims about products and supply chains. Software and data tools support these services, and AI is used to process large amounts of supplier and energy data, estimate emissions where measured data is missing, and identify the best reduction opportunities.

item.title: Climate FieldView
item.description:
Climate FieldView helps farmers use their data. With a device plugged into farm equipment, FieldView Drive collects information about planting, applications, and harvest, and the data syncs to the cloud, where farmers view maps of their fields, compare hybrids and practices, and analyze yield. Satellite imagery tracks crop health during the season, and weather data and field notes add context.

Advanced features support planning. Variable-rate prescriptions tell equipment to apply seed and fertilizer at different rates across a field based on zones, which can improve efficiency, and scripts or models estimate the profitability of decisions. Integrations with equipment and other agriculture software reduce manual data transfers. Machine learning supports yield predictions and recommendations.

item.title: Climate TRACE
item.description: Climate TRACE exists because official emissions reporting is slow and incomplete. The coalition combines satellite images, sensor data, and public records and applies machine learning to estimate emissions from individual sources: power plants, steel mills, oil and gas fields, ships, aircraft, cement plants, farms, and more. The result is a global inventory that can be searched by country, sector, or even a single facility, updated more frequently than government reports.

item.title: FarmLogs
item.description:
FarmLogs began as a way for farmers to keep records digitally instead of in notebooks. Growers could map their fields, log planting, spraying, and harvest activities, track inputs and costs, and see weather and satellite imagery for each field. The aim was to make it easier to understand what was working in a season, to meet record-keeping requirements, and to share information with advisors and landlords.

The product became part of Bushel, a company that provides software for grain buyers, farmers, and the supply chain. Under the name Bushel Farm, it connects farmers with grain markets and elevators, shows contract and delivery information, and supports tools for tracking grain inventory. Data from fields and grain marketing is brought into one view, and analytics help evaluate profitability.

item.title: Granular
item.description:
Granular was built to help large farm operations plan and track their business. Its software covered field activity and agronomy, inventory, labor, equipment, and financial reporting, and tried to give farm managers a view of costs and profitability for each crop and field. Corteva Agriscience acquired it, and for several years it was marketed to commercial growers who wanted enterprise-level tools.

The product line has since been restructured. Corteva discontinued Granular Agronomy, the field-level software, and sold the financial and business-management side to a company called Traction Ag. The pieces now go by different names and are maintained by different companies, which makes it important to confirm what is currently offered under the Granular name.

item.title: John Deere Operations Center
item.description:
The Operations Center connects Deere equipment to farm management. Tractors, planters, sprayers, and combines send data about where they worked, what they applied, and how crops yielded, and farmers see this on field maps. Records of planting, spraying, and harvest are kept in one place and can be shared with advisors.

From that data, the platform helps plan the next season. Prescriptions vary seed or fertilizer rates across a field, and analytics compare performance between fields and years. Integrations with other agronomy software and equipment from other makers extend its reach, and AI is used for tasks such as image-based crop and weed detection on machines.

item.title: Planet Labs
item.description: Planet Labs built its business on frequency. Rather than a few large satellites, it operates a large number of small ones, so it can photograph almost every part of the land surface regularly. That consistency allows users to watch change over time: crops growing, forests being cleared, ice melting, construction progressing, or ships moving. The imagery has a lower resolution than the sharpest commercial satellites but far greater frequency, and some higher-resolution satellites supplement it.

item.title: Watershed
item.description:
Watershed focuses on carbon accounting for large companies. Organizations connect data from finance systems, energy bills, travel, and suppliers, and the platform converts that activity data into greenhouse gas emissions across all scopes, including the harder-to-measure supply chain. The methods follow recognized standards and are designed to stand up to audits, which matters as more companies face disclosure rules.

Beyond measurement, the platform supports action. Companies set targets, model reduction scenarios, and track progress, and tools for engaging suppliers help gather better data and cut emissions in the value chain. Reporting features produce disclosures for frameworks and regulations, and AI helps classify purchases, fill gaps in data, and prepare reports, which reduces the manual effort that carbon accounting requires.
